items.title: Lesson 3 Focus Question: How can you design a circuit so that several lamps in a workshop can be switched on and off independently?

answer.html: Wire the lamps in parallel, each with its own switch in series with that lamp. Each lamp then has the full source voltage, and opening one switch does not affect the others. (A series connection would make every lamp share one current and go out together.) Calculate the equivalent resistance and use 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅 to check the total current.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (a): Describe a series circuit using a string of four lamps. What happens to the other lamps if one is unscrewed?

answer.html: A series circuit has only one path for the current, so the same current goes through all four lamps one after another. Unscrewing one lamp opens the only path, so all the lamps go out.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 21: In a voltage-divider diagram with a 12-V battery and two resistors in series, explain why the current arrow leaves the battery's top (+) terminal

answer.html: Conventional current is the direction a positive charge would move, so it leaves the battery's positive terminal, passes through both resistors one after the other, and returns to the negative terminal.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 24, Get It? (b): In a parallel circuit diagram, a circled V is across a lamp and a circled A is in the wire leaving the battery. What do the symbols mean?

answer.html: The circled V is a voltmeter, connected in parallel to read the potential difference across the lamp. The circled A is an ammeter, connected in series to read the total current leaving the battery.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (c): A 20-Ω resistor carries 0.30 A. Name two changes that would double the current

body.html: The current depends on the potential difference and the resistance: 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅.

answer.html: Double the potential difference across the resistor (from 6.0 V to 12 V), or replace it with a resistor of half the resistance (10 Ω) at the same voltage.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (d): A charge gains 9.0 V from a battery and then passes through two resistors in series. Explain, using energy conservation, how the drops must compare to 9.0 V

answer.html: The charge returns to its starting point, so its potential energy cannot have changed over the full loop. The energy it gains from the battery must equal the energy it gives up in the resistors, so the two drops add up to 9.0 V.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (e): Use the loop rule to find the missing drop. A 12-V battery drives a loop in which one resistor drops 5.0 V and a second resistor is the only other element

body.html: Going once around a closed loop, the sum of the potential increases equals the sum of the potential decreases.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 7.0 V

items.title: 42: Four 27-Ω resistors are connected in series across a 110-V generator. Find the equivalent resistance and the current

body.html: 𝑅<sub>1</sub> = 𝑅<sub>2</sub> = 𝑅<sub>3</sub> = 𝑅<sub>4</sub> = 27 𝛺, 𝛥𝑉= 110 V. Find 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> and 𝐼.
In series, resistances add, and the current is the same everywhere: 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> = 108 𝛺, 𝐼≈1.0 A

check.html: The equivalent resistance exceeds any single resistor.

items.title: 43: 18-Ω, 27-Ω and 9.0-Ω resistors are in series with a 90-V battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the current

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> = 54 𝛺, 𝐼≈1.7 A

items.title: 44: A string of 20 identical bulbs in series is connected to 120 V and carries 0.25 A. What is the resistance of each bulb?

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 120 V, 𝐼= 0.25 A, 20 equal bulbs.

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>bulb</sub> = 24 𝛺

check.html: Each bulb drops 6.0 V, and twenty of them add up to 120 V.

items.title: 45: A 6.0-V battery has two resistors in series. One resistor is replaced by a smaller one. (a) What happens to the equivalent resistance? (b) To the current? (c) Does the battery voltage change?

body.html: 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> = 𝑅<sub>1</sub> + 𝑅<sub>2</sub>, 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>, and the battery voltage is set by the battery itself. (a) If one resistance decreases, the sum decreases.

answer.html: The equivalent resistance decreases. (b) With the same battery voltage and smaller 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>, 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> gets larger.
The current increases. (c) The (ideal) battery maintains its voltage.
No. The battery voltage stays 6.0 V.

items.title: 46 (Challenge): Find the potential difference across each of the 18-Ω, 27-Ω and 9.0-Ω resistors in series with a 90-V battery, and verify that they add to the battery voltage

body.html: The current is the same in each; use 𝛥𝑉= 𝐼𝑅 for each resistor, with 𝐼= 90 / 54 = 1.667 A from Problem 43.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>18</sub> = 30 V, 𝛥𝑉<sub>27</sub> = 45 V, 𝛥𝑉<sub>9</sub> = 15 V. Their sum is 90 V, equal to the battery's potential difference (the loop rule is verified).

items.title: 47: Two resistors 𝑅1 and 𝑅2 are in series with an ammeter and a 90-V battery. Voltmeter 𝑉1 is across 𝑅1 and 𝑉2 is across 𝑅2. The ammeter reads 0 A, 𝑉1 reads 90 V and 𝑉2 reads 0 V. What happened?

body.html: Zero current means the loop is open somewhere. A resistor that carries no current has no voltage drop (𝐼𝑅= 0), unless it is the open part itself.

𝑅<sub>2</sub> has no drop, as expected for any resistor in a loop with a break elsewhere. The voltmeter across 𝑅<sub>1</sub> reads the full 90 V. Across a break, the voltmeter completes the circuit through its enormous resistance and takes essentially all of the battery voltage, while the tiny current drops almost nothing across 𝑅<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>1</sub> has failed open (its filament or wire is broken), so there is a gap in the loop at 𝑅<sub>1</sub>.

check.html: If 𝑅<sub>2</sub> had opened instead, the readings would be 𝛥𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 0 and 𝛥𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 90 V.

body.html: 𝑅<sub>1</sub>, 𝑅<sub>2</sub>, 𝛥𝑉<sub>1</sub> only.
(a) 𝐼=<sub> </sub><sup>𝛥</sup><sup>𝑉</sup><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝑅</sup><sub>1</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>15</sup><sup> </sup><sup>V</sup> <sub>180</sub><sub> </sub><sub>𝛺</sub>= 0.0833 A

answer.html: 𝑃<sub>1</sub> ≈1.3 W, 𝑃<sub>2</sub> ≈2.3 W, 𝑃<sub>total</sub> ≈3.5 W (d) 1.25 + 2.29 = 3.54 W, which equals the total.
Yes. Energy is conserved: all the power the battery supplies is used by the two resistors, so 𝑃<sub>total</sub> = 𝑃<sub>1</sub> + 𝑃<sub>2</sub>.

items.title: 49: A string of 40 identical series lamps, each 10.0 Ω when hot, is on 120 V. Each lamp has a shunt that shorts it out if its filament breaks. After 12 lamps have shorted, what is the current, and what voltage does each remaining lamp get? Why might a 0.40-A fuse blow?

body.html: In a series string, a broken filament would open the loop, but a shunt lets the current pass. A shorted lamp removes its resistance, so 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> falls and the current 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> rises.
Before any failure: 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> = 40(10.0 𝛺) = 400 𝛺,
After 12 lamps short out, 28 remain:

answer.html: The current rises from 0.300 A to 0.429 A, and each remaining lamp gets 4.29 V instead of 3.00 V, so it is hotter and brighter (its power rises from 0.90 W to 1.84 W). The current of 0.429 A is greater than the 0.40-A fuse rating, so the fuse blows.

items.title: 50: A 20-Ω and a 60-Ω resistor are in series and carry 0.50 A. Which gets hotter, and by what factor?

body.html: The resistors are in series, so they carry the same current 𝐼. Power (heating) is 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅.

answer.html: The 60-Ω resistor gets hotter. With equal current, its power (15 W) is three times that of the 20-Ω resistor (5.0 W), the same ratio as the resistances.

items.title: 51 (Challenge): A 9.0-V battery is in series with four resistors. The drops across three of them are 1.4 V, 2.6 V and 3.1 V. What is the voltage across the fourth?

body.html: Loop rule: the drops add to the source voltage.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>4</sub> = 1.9 V

items.title: 58 (Challenge): A branch has a 220-Ω resistor. What resistor must be added, and how connected, to reduce the branch's resistance to 140 Ω?

body.html: Adding resistance in series can only increase the resistance, so to lower it you must add a resistor in parallel with the 220-Ω resistor.

answer.html: Use a resistor of about 3.9 × 10<sup>2</sup> 𝛺 (385 Ω), connected in parallel with the 220-Ω resistor.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress Problem 59: A string of lamps is wired once in series and once in parallel, and one lamp is then removed from each. Compare what happens to the voltages, currents and brightness of the remaining lamps

question.html: Series Parallel Current The same through every lamp; drops to zero if one is removed Splits among branches; the other branches are unchanged Voltage
The same across every branch (the full source voltage) Remaining lamps All go out Keep their brightness

answer.html: In series, removing a lamp opens the only path, so all lamps go out. In parallel, the other lamps still have the full source voltage and the same current, so they stay equally bright.

items.title: 60: Parallel branch currents are 45 mA, 0.18 A, 320 mA and 1.4 A. What is the current through the source?

body.html: Junction rule: the total current is the sum of the branch currents.

items.title: 61: A series circuit has five resistors, and one of them carries 2.4 mA. What is the current through the source?

answer.html: 2.4 mA. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, including through the source.

items.title: 62: A switch is in series with a 100-W bulb on 115 V. What is the voltage across the switch (a) when it is closed and (b) when it is open?

body.html: In series, the voltages add to 115 V. A closed switch is just wire with essentially zero resistance. An open switch is a gap with enormous resistance that carries essentially all the voltage.

answer.html: When closed, 𝛥𝑉<sub>switch</sub> ≈0 V (the bulb gets the full 115 V).
When open, 𝛥𝑉<sub>switch</sub> = 115 V (no current, so there is no drop across the bulb).

items.title: 63: Compare the loop rule to riding a roller coaster around a closed track

answer.html: A coaster that returns to its starting point has risen exactly as much as it has dropped, so its net change in height (and gravitational potential energy) is zero. In the same way, a charge going around a closed loop returns to its starting potential, so the total rise in potential (across batteries) equals the total drop (across resistors).

items.title: 64: Water flows through a pipe that splits into three smaller pipes. Explain how this is like the junction rule for currents

answer.html: Water is not created, destroyed or stored at the split, so the flow into the junction equals the total flow out through the three pipes. Likewise charge cannot be created, destroyed or piled up at a junction, so the sum of the currents into a junction equals the sum of the currents out.

items.title: 65 (Critical Thinking): Four identical 20.0-Ω resistors are connected to a 12.0-V battery as two parallel branches, each with two resistors in series. A and B are the midpoints of the two branches. A wire is added from A to B

body.html: Each branch divides the battery voltage equally between its two equal resistors, so A and B are both at the same potential (half-way between the battery terminals). A wire joining points at equal potential has no voltage across it. Work (before the wire): Each branch has 𝑅= 40.0 𝛺, so the branch current is 12.0 / 40.0 = 0.300 A and the battery current is 0.600 A. (a) Zero current, because there is no potential difference between A and B.

answer.html: The current through the wire is zero. (b) Each resistor still has 6.0 V across it, so each still carries 6.0 / 20.0 = 0.300 A.

The current through each resistor does not change (0.300 A). (c) With the wire, two 10.0 𝛺 pairs are in series: 𝑅<sub>total</sub> = 20.0 𝛺 (the same as two 40.0 𝛺 branches in parallel), so 𝐼= 12.0 / 20.0 = 0.600 A.
The current through the battery does not change (0.600 A). (d)
The potential difference across each resistor does not change (6.0 V).

items.title: Lesson 3 Focus Question: How can you build a simple circuit to fit the needs of a given situation?

answer.html: Choose the connection that gives the behavior you need. Use a series connection when the devices must share one current (or when you need a voltage divider or a single on/off control). Use a parallel connection when each device needs the full source voltage and must work independently, as in household wiring. Calculate the equivalent resistance, then use 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅 to check the current.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (a): Define "series circuit"

answer.html: A circuit with only one path for the current, so the same current goes through every component.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 21: Explain why the current arrow in the voltage-divider diagram points the way it does

answer.html: Conventional current is the direction a positive charge would move, so it leaves the battery's positive terminal, passes through 𝑅<sub>1</sub> and 𝑅<sub>2</sub>, and returns to the negative terminal.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 24, Get It? (b): What do the symbols V and A mean in the circuit?

answer.html: The circled V is a voltmeter (measures potential difference across a component, here 120 V across each resistor). The circled A is an ammeter (measures the current through that part of the circuit).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (c): Identify the two factors on which the current through a resistor depends

answer.html: The potential difference across the resistor and the resistance of the resistor (𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (d): Explain how Kirchhoff's loop rule and conservation of energy are related

answer.html: A charge going around a closed loop returns to its starting point, so its potential energy cannot have changed. Energy conservation therefore requires that the total potential rise (from sources) equals the total potential drop (across devices), which is the loop rule.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (e): State the loop rule in your own words

answer.html: Going once around any closed loop, the sum of the potential increases equals the sum of the potential decreases (the net change in potential is zero).

items.title: 42: Three 22-Ω resistors in series across a 125-V generator

body.html: 𝑅<sub>1</sub> = 𝑅<sub>2</sub> = 𝑅<sub>3</sub> = 22 𝛺, 𝛥𝑉= 125 V. Find 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> and 𝐼.
In series, resistances add, and the current is the same everywhere: 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> = 66 𝛺, 𝐼≈1.9 A

answer.html: The equivalent resistance increases. (b) With the same battery voltage and larger 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>, 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> gets smaller.
The current decreases. (c) The (ideal) battery maintains its voltage.

items.title: 46 (Challenge): Potential differences across 12-Ω, 15-Ω and 5-Ω resistors in series with a 75-V battery

body.html: The current is the same in each; use 𝛥𝑉= 𝐼𝑅 for each resistor, with 𝐼= 75 / 32 = 2.344 A from Problem 43.

answer.html: 𝛥𝑉<sub>12</sub> ≈28 V, 𝛥𝑉<sub>15</sub> ≈35 V, 𝛥𝑉<sub>5</sub> ≈12 V. Their sum is 75 V, equal to the battery's potential difference (the loop rule is verified).

items.title: 47: Example Problem 4 circuit shows ammeter 0 A, 𝛥𝑉1 = 0 V, 𝛥𝑉2 = 45 V. What happened?

body.html: Zero current means the loop is open somewhere. A resistor with no current has no voltage drop across it (𝐼𝑅= 0), unless it is the open part itself.

𝑅<sub>1</sub> has no current and no drop, which is expected for any break in the loop. If 𝑅<sub>1</sub> were the open part, the voltmeter across it would read the full 45 V. Instead, the voltmeter across 𝑅<sub>2</sub> reads 45 V: across a break, the voltmeter completes the circuit through its enormous resistance and takes the full battery voltage, while the tiny current drops almost nothing across 𝑅<sub>1</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑅<sub>2</sub> has failed open (its filament or wire is broken), so there is a gap in the loop at 𝑅<sub>2</sub>.

check.html: If 𝑅<sub>1</sub> had opened instead, the readings would be 𝛥𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 45 V and 𝛥𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 0.

(a) 𝐼=<sub> </sub><sup>𝛥</sup><sup>𝑉</sup><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝑅</sup><sub>1</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>17</sup><sup> </sup><sup>V</sup> <sub>255</sub><sub> </sub><sub>𝛺</sub>= 0.0667 A

answer.html: 𝑃<sub>1</sub> ≈1.1 W, 𝑃<sub>2</sub> ≈1.3 W, 𝑃<sub>total</sub> ≈2.4 W (d) 1.13 + 1.29 = 2.42 W, which equals the total.
Yes. Energy is conserved: all the power the battery supplies is used by the two resistors, so 𝑃<sub>total</sub> = 𝑃<sub>1</sub> + 𝑃<sub>2</sub>.

items.title: 49: Why do holiday-light lamps short out at line voltage, and why might a fuse blow after many bulbs have failed?

body.html: In a series string, one burned-out filament opens the whole loop and all the lights go out. The special lamps have a shunt that becomes a conductor when the voltage across them rises to the full line voltage (which is what happens across a lamp with a broken filament, because it now carries all of the voltage of the open loop).

The shorted lamp passes current, so the rest of the string lights again. But each shorted lamp removes its resistance, so 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> falls. The same line voltage across a smaller 𝑅<sub>eq</sub> gives a larger current 𝐼= 𝛥𝑉/ 𝑅<sub>eq</sub>, and the remaining bulbs each carry a larger voltage and are heated more. After enough bulbs fail, the current exceeds the fuse rating.

answer.html: The lamp shorts out so that the broken bulb no longer opens the circuit. Fuses blow after many bulbs have failed because each shorted bulb lowers the string's total resistance, so the current at fixed line voltage rises above the fuse's rating.

items.title: 50: Why does the lower-resistance resistor in Example Problem 4 run cooler?

body.html: The resistors are in series, so they carry the same current 𝐼. Power (heating) is 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅.

answer.html: With equal current, 𝑃= 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 is smaller for the smaller resistance, so that resistor converts less electrical energy to thermal energy each second and stays cooler.

items.title: 62: A switch in series with a 75-W bulb on 120 V

body.html: In series, the voltages add to 120 V. A closed switch is just wire, with essentially zero resistance. An open switch is a gap with enormous resistance that carries essentially all the voltage.

answer.html: When closed, 𝛥𝑉<sub>switch</sub> ≈0 V (the bulb gets the full 120 V).
When open, 𝛥𝑉<sub>switch</sub> = 120 V (no current, so there is no drop across the bulb).

items.title: 63: Compare the loop rule to hiking around a hill

answer.html: If you hike in a loop and return to your start, your total climb equals your total descent. In the same way, a charge going around a closed loop returns to its starting potential, so the total rise in potential (across batteries) equals the total drop (across resistors). Elevation corresponds to electric potential.

items.title: 64: How does the junction rule relate to conservation of charge?

answer.html: Charge cannot be created, destroyed, or piled up at a junction. So every coulomb per second that enters a junction must leave it: the sum of currents in equals the sum of currents out.

items.title: 65 (Critical Thinking): Figure 27, four identical resistors, wire added from A to B

question.html: The circuit is two parallel branches, each with two identical resistors in series; A and B are the midpoints of the two branches.

body.html: Each branch divides the battery voltage equally between its two equal resistors, so A and B are both at the same potential (half-way between the two battery terminals). A wire joining points at equal potential has no voltage across it. (a) Zero current, because there is no potential difference between A and B.

answer.html: The current through the wire is zero. (b) Each resistor still has the same voltage (𝑉/ 2) across it, so its current is unchanged.
The current through each resistor does not change. (c) The total resistance is unchanged (two 2𝑅 branches in parallel give 𝑅; with the wire, two 𝑅/ 2 pairs in series also give 𝑅).
The current through the battery does not change. (d)
The potential difference across each resistor does not change (each stays at 𝑉/ 2).
